L24: # CreateRestrictedToken function (securitybaseapi.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: The CreateRestrictedToken function creates a new 【5†access token】 that is a restricted version of an existing access token. The restricted token can have disabled 【6†security identifiers】 (SIDs), deleted privileges, and a list of restricting SIDs. For more information, see 【7†Restricted Tokens】.
L33: ## Syntax
L34: 
L35:     `BOOL CreateRestrictedToken(
L36:       [in]           HANDLE               ExistingTokenHandle,
L37:       [in]           DWORD                Flags,
L38:       [in]           DWORD                DisableSidCount,
L39:       [in, optional] PSID_AND_ATTRIBUTES  SidsToDisable,
L40:       [in]           DWORD                DeletePrivilegeCount,
L41:       [in, optional] PLUID_AND_ATTRIBUTES PrivilegesToDelete,
L42:       [in]           DWORD                RestrictedSidCount,
L43:       [in, optional] PSID_AND_ATTRIBUTES  SidsToRestrict,
L44:       [out]          PHANDLE              NewTokenHandle
L45:     );
L46:     `
L47: ## Parameters
L48: 
L49: `[in] ExistingTokenHandle`
L50: 
L51: A handle to a 【8†primary】 or 【9†impersonation token】. The token can also be a restricted token. The handle must have TOKEN_DUPLICATE access to the token.
L52: 
L53: `[in] Flags`
L54: 
L55: Specifies additional privilege options. This parameter can be zero or a combination of the following values.
L56: Value  | Meaning
L57: --- | ---
L58: DISABLE_MAX_PRIVILEGE
L59: `0x1`  | Disables all privileges in the new token except the SeChangeNotifyPrivilege privilege. If this value is specified, the DeletePrivilegeCount and PrivilegesToDelete parameters are ignored.
L60: SANDBOX_INERT
L61: `0x2`  | If this value is used, the system does not check 【10†AppLocker】 rules or apply 【11†Software Restriction Policies】. For 【10†AppLocker】, this flag disables checks for all four rule collections: Executable, Windows Installer, Script, and DLL.
L62: When creating a setup program that must run extracted DLLs during installation, use the flag SAFER_TOKEN_MAKE_INERT in the 【12†SaferComputeTokenFromLevel】 function.
L63: A token can be queried for existence of this flag by using 【13†GetTokenInformation】.
L64: Windows Server 2008 R2, Windows 7, Windows Server 2008, Windows Vista, Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP: On systems with KB2532445 installed, the caller must be running as LocalSystem or TrustedInstaller or the system ignores this flag. For more information, see 【14†You can circumvent AppLocker rules by using an Office macro on a computer that is running Windows 7 or Windows Server 2008 R2†support.microsoft.com】.
L65: Windows Server 2008, Windows Vista, Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP: AppLocker is not supported. AppLocker was introduced in Windows 7 and Windows Server 2008 R2.
L66: LUA_TOKEN
L67: `0x4`  | The new token is a LUA token.
L68: Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP: This value is not supported.
L69: WRITE_RESTRICTED
L70: `0x8`  | The new token contains restricting SIDs that are considered only when evaluating write access.
L71: Windows XP with SP2 and later: The value of this constant is `0x4`. For an application to be compatible with Windows XP with SP2 and later operating systems, the application should query the operating system by calling the 【15†GetVersionEx】 function to determine which value should be used.
L72: Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP with SP1 and earlier: This value is not supported.
L73: `[in] DisableSidCount`
L74: 
L75: Specifies the number of entries in the SidsToDisable array.
L76: 
L77: `[in, optional] SidsToDisable`
L78: 
L79: A pointer to an array of 【16†SID_AND_ATTRIBUTES】 structures that specify the deny-only SIDs in the restricted token. The system uses a deny-only SID to deny access to a securable object. The absence of a deny-only SID does not allow access.
L80: 
L81: Disabling a SID turns on SE_GROUP_USE_FOR_DENY_ONLY and turns off SE_GROUP_ENABLED and SE_GROUP_ENABLED_BY_DEFAULT. All other attributes are ignored.
L82: Deny-only attributes apply to any combination of an existing token's SIDs, including the user SID and group SIDs that have the SE_GROUP_MANDATORY attribute. To get the SIDs associated with the existing token, use the 【13†GetTokenInformation】 function with the TokenUser and TokenGroups flags. The function ignores any SIDs in the array that are not also found in the existing token.
L83: 
L84: The function ignores the Attributes member of the 【16†SID_AND_ATTRIBUTES】 structure.
L85: This parameter can be NULL if no SIDs are to be disabled.
L86: 
L87: `[in] DeletePrivilegeCount`
L88: 
L89: Specifies the number of entries in the PrivilegesToDelete array.
L90: 
L91: `[in, optional] PrivilegesToDelete`
L92: 
L93: A pointer to an array of 【17†LUID_AND_ATTRIBUTES】 structures that specify the privileges to delete in the restricted token.
L94: The 【13†GetTokenInformation】 function can be used with the TokenPrivileges flag to retrieve the privileges held by the existing token. The function ignores any privileges in the array that are not held by the existing token.
L95: 
L96: The function ignores the Attributes members of the 【17†LUID_AND_ATTRIBUTES】 structures.
L97: 
L98: This parameter can be NULL if you do not want to delete any privileges.
L99: 
L100: If the calling program passes too many privileges in this array, CreateRestrictedToken returns ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER.
L101: `[in] RestrictedSidCount`
L102: 
L103: Specifies the number of entries in the SidsToRestrict array.
L104: 
L105: `[in, optional] SidsToRestrict`
L106: A pointer to an array of 【16†SID_AND_ATTRIBUTES】 structures that specify a list of restricting SIDs for the new token. If the existing token is a restricted token, the list of restricting SIDs for the new token is the intersection of this array and the list of restricting SIDs for the existing token. No check is performed to remove duplicate SIDs that were placed on the SidsToRestrict parameter. Duplicate SIDs allow a restricted token to have redundant information in the restricting SID list.
L107: The Attributes member of the 【16†SID_AND_ATTRIBUTES】 structure must be zero. Restricting SIDs are always enabled for access checks.
L108: 
L109: This parameter can be NULL if you do not want to specify any restricting SIDs.
L110: 
L111: `[out] NewTokenHandle`
L112: A pointer to a variable that receives a handle to the new restricted token. This handle has the same access rights as ExistingTokenHandle. The new token is the same type, 【8†primary】 or 【9†impersonation】, as the existing token. The handle returned in NewTokenHandle can be duplicated.
L113: ## Return value
L114: 
L115: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero.
L116: 
L117: If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call 【18†GetLastError】.
L118: ## Remarks
L119: 
L120: The CreateRestrictedToken function can restrict the token in the following ways:
L121:   * Apply the deny-only attribute to SIDs in the token so they cannot be used to access secured objects. For more information about the deny-only attribute, see 【19†SID Attributes in an Access Token】.
L122:   * Remove 【20†privileges】 from the token.
L123:   * Specify a list of restricting SIDs, which the system uses when it checks the token's access to a securable object. The system performs two access checks: one using the token's enabled SIDs, and another using the list of restricting SIDs. Access is granted only if both access checks allow the requested access rights.
L124: You can use the restricted token in the 【21†CreateProcessAsUser】 function to create a process that has restricted access rights and privileges. If a process calls CreateProcessAsUser using a restricted version of its own token, the calling process does not need to have the SE_ASSIGNPRIMARYTOKEN_NAME privilege.
L125: 
L126: You can use the restricted token in the 【22†ImpersonateLoggedOnUser】 function.
L127: 
L128: Warning
L129: Applications that use restricted tokens should run the restricted application on desktops other than the default desktop. This is necessary to prevent an attack by a restricted application, using SendMessage or PostMessage, to unrestricted applications on the default desktop. If necessary, switch between desktops for your application purposes.
L130: ## Requirements
L131: 
L132: Requirement  | Value
L133: --- | ---
L134: Minimum supported client  | Windows XP [desktop apps only]
L135: Minimum supported server  | Windows Server 2003 [desktop apps only]
L136: Target Platform  | Windows
L137: Header  | securitybaseapi.h (include Windows.h)
L138: Library  | Advapi32.lib
L139: DLL  | Advapi32.dll

L24: # DeleteFileW function (fileapi.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: Deletes an existing file.
L33: 
L34: To perform this operation as a transacted operation, use the 【5†DeleteFileTransacted】 function.
L35: 
L36: ## Syntax
L37: 
L38:     `BOOL DeleteFileW(
L39:       [in] LPCWSTR lpFileName
L40:     );
L41:     `
L42: ## Parameters
L43: 
L44: `[in] lpFileName`
L45: 
L46: The name of the file to be deleted.
L47: 
L48: By default, the name is limited to MAX_PATH characters. To extend this limit to 32,767 wide characters, prepend "\\?\" to the path. For more information, see 【6†Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces】.
L49: 
L50: Tip
L51: 
L52: Starting with Windows 10, Version 1607, you can opt-in to remove the MAX_PATH limitation without prepending "\\?\". See the "Maximum Path Length Limitation" section of 【6†Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces】 for details.
L53: ## Return value
L54: 
L55: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero.
L56: 
L57: If the function fails, the return value is zero (0). To get extended error information, call 【7†GetLastError】.
L58: ## Remarks
L59: 
L60: If an application attempts to delete a file that does not exist, the DeleteFile function fails with ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND. If the file is a read-only file, the function fails with ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED.
L61: 
L62: The following list identifies some tips for deleting, removing, or closing files:
L63:   * To delete a read-only file, first you must remove the read-only attribute.
L64:   * To delete or rename a file, you must have either delete permission on the file, or delete child permission in the parent directory.
L65:   * To recursively delete the files in a directory, use the 【8†SHFileOperation】 function.
L66:   * To remove an empty directory, use the 【9†RemoveDirectory】 function.
L67:   * To close an open file, use the 【10†CloseHandle】 function.
L68: If you set up a directory with all access except delete and delete child, and the access control lists (ACL) of new files are inherited, then you can create a file without being able to delete it. However, then you can create a file, and then get all the access you request on the handle that is returned to you at the time you create the file.
L69: If you request delete permission at the time you create a file, you can delete or rename the file with that handle, but not with any other handle. For more information, see 【11†File Security and Access Rights】.
L70: 
L71: The DeleteFile function fails if an application attempts to delete a file that has other handles open for normal I/O or as a memory-mapped file (FILE_SHARE_DELETE must have been specified when other handles were opened).
L72: The DeleteFile function marks a file for deletion on close. Therefore, the file deletion does not occur until the last handle to the file is closed. Subsequent calls to 【12†CreateFile】 to open the file fail with ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED.
L73: 
L74: The use of POSIX delete causes the file to be deleted while handles remain open. Subsequent calls to 【12†CreateFile】 to open the file fail with ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND.
L75: 
L76: Symbolic link behavior:
L77: If the path points to a symbolic link, the symbolic link is deleted, not the target. To delete a target, you must call 【12†CreateFile】 and specify FILE_FLAG_DELETE_ON_CLOSE.
L78: 
L79: In Windows 8 and Windows Server 2012, this function is supported by the following technologies:
L80: Technology  | Supported
L81: --- | ---
L82: Server Message Block (SMB) 3.0 protocol  | Yes
L83: SMB 3.0 Transparent Failover (TFO)  | Yes
L84: SMB 3.0 with Scale-out File Shares (SO)  | Yes
L85: Cluster Shared Volume File System (CsvFS)  | Yes
L86: Resilient File System (ReFS)  | Yes
L87: #### Examples
L88: 
L89: For an example, see 【13†Locking and Unlocking Byte Ranges in Files】.
L90: 
L91: Note
L92: 
L93: The `fileapi.h` header defines DeleteFile as an alias that automatically selects the ANSI or Unicode version of this function based on the definition of the UNICODE preprocessor constant. Mixing usage of the encoding-neutral alias with code that is not encoding-neutral can lead to mismatches that result in compilation or runtime errors. For more information, see 【14†Conventions for Function Prototypes】.
L94: ## Requirements
L95: 
L96: Requirement  | Value
L97: --- | ---
L98: Minimum supported client  | Windows XP [desktop apps | UWP apps]
L99: Minimum supported server  | Windows Server 2003 [desktop apps | UWP apps]
L100: Target Platform  | Windows
L101: Header  | fileapi.h (include Windows.h)
L102: Library  | Kernel32.lib
L103: DLL  | Kernel32.dll

L24: # File security and access rights
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: Because files are 【5†securable objects】, access to them is regulated by the access-control model that governs access to all other securable objects in Windows. For a detailed explanation of this model, see 【6†Access Control】.
L33: ## Security descriptors
L34: You can specify a 【7†security descriptor】 for a file or directory when you call the 【8†CreateFile】, 【9†CreateDirectory】, or 【10†CreateDirectoryEx】 function. If you specify `NULL` for the lpSecurityAttributes parameter, the file or directory gets a default security descriptor. The access control lists (ACL) in the default security descriptor for a file or directory are inherited from its parent directory.
L35: Note that a default security descriptor is assigned only when a file or directory is newly created, and not when it is renamed or moved.
L36: To retrieve the security descriptor of a file or directory object, call the 【11†GetNamedSecurityInfo】 or 【12†GetSecurityInfo】 function. To change the security descriptor of a file or directory object, call the 【13†SetNamedSecurityInfo】 or 【14†SetSecurityInfo】 function.
L37: ## File access rights
L38: 
L39: The valid access rights for files and directories include the DELETE, READ_CONTROL, WRITE_DAC, WRITE_OWNER, and SYNCHRONIZE 【15†standard access rights】. The table in 【16†File Access Rights Constants】 lists the access rights that are specific to files and directories.
L40: Although the SYNCHRONIZE access right is defined within the 【15†standard access rights】 list as the right to specify a file handle in one of the wait functions, when using asynchronous file I/O operations you should wait on the event handle contained in a properly configured 【17†OVERLAPPED】 structure rather than using the file handle with the SYNCHRONIZE access right for synchronization.
L41: 
L42: The following are the 【18†generic access rights】 for files and directories:
L43: Generic access right  | Mapped access rights  | Generic meaning
L44: --- | --- | ---
L45: FILE_GENERIC_EXECUTE  | FILE_EXECUTE
L46: FILE_READ_ATTRIBUTES
L47: STANDARD_RIGHTS_EXECUTE
L48: SYNCHRONIZE  | Execute access
L49: FILE_GENERIC_READ  | FILE_READ_ATTRIBUTES
L50: FILE_READ_DATA
L51: FILE_READ_EA
L52: STANDARD_RIGHTS_READ
L53: SYNCHRONIZE  | Read access
L54: FILE_GENERIC_WRITE  | FILE_APPEND_DATA
L55: FILE_WRITE_ATTRIBUTES
L56: FILE_WRITE_DATA
L57: FILE_WRITE_EA
L58: STANDARD_RIGHTS_WRITE
L59: SYNCHRONIZE  | Write access
L60: Windows compares the requested access rights and the information in the thread's access token with the information in the file or directory object's security descriptor. If the comparison does not prohibit all of the requested access rights from being granted, a handle to the object is returned to the thread and the access rights are granted. For more information about this process, see 【19†Interaction between Threads and Securable Objects】.
L61: By default, authorization for access to a file or directory is controlled strictly by the ACLs in the security descriptor associated with that file or directory. In particular, the security descriptor of a parent directory is not used to control access to any child file or directory. The FILE_TRAVERSE 【20†access right】 can be enforced by removing the BYPASS_TRAVERSE_CHECKING 【21†privilege】 from users.
L62: This is not recommended in the general case, as many programs do not correctly handle directory traversal errors. The primary use for the FILE_TRAVERSE access right on directories is to enable conformance to certain IEEE and ISO POSIX standards when interoperability with Unix systems is a requirement.
L63: The Windows security model provides a way for a child directory to inherit, or to be prevented from inheriting, one or more of the ACEs in the parent directory's security descriptor. Each ACE contains information that determines how it can be inherited, and whether it will have an effect on the inheriting directory object. For example, some inherited ACEs control access to the inherited directory object, and these are called effective ACEs. All other ACEs are called inherit-only ACEs.
L64: The Windows security model also enforces the automatic inheritance of ACEs to child objects according to the 【22†ACE inheritance rules】. This automatic inheritance, along with the inheritance information in each ACE, determines how security restrictions are passed down the directory hierarchy.
L65: Note that you cannot use an access-denied ACE to deny only GENERIC_READ or only GENERIC_WRITE access to a file. This is because for file objects, the generic mappings for both GENERIC_READ or GENERIC_WRITE include the SYNCHRONIZE access right. If an ACE denies GENERIC_WRITE access to a trustee, and the trustee requests GENERIC_READ access, the request will fail because the request implicitly includes SYNCHRONIZE access which is implicitly denied by the ACE, and vice versa.
L66: Instead of using access-denied ACEs, use access-allowed ACEs to explicitly allow the permitted access rights.
L67: Another means of managing access to storage objects is encryption. The implementation of file system encryption in Windows is the Encrypted File System, or EFS. EFS encrypts only files and not directories. The advantage of encryption is that it provides additional protection to files that is applied on the media and not through the file system and the standard Windows access control architecture. For more information on file encryption, see 【23†File Encryption】.
L68: ## Backup and restore access rights
L69: In most cases, the ability to read and write the security settings of a file or directory object is restricted to kernel-mode processes. Clearly, you would not want any user process to be able to change the ownership or access restriction on your private file or directory. However, a backup application would not be able to complete its job of backing up your file if the access restrictions you have placed on your file or directory does not allow the application's user-mode process to read it.
L70: Backup applications must be able to override the security settings of file and directory objects to ensure a complete backup. Similarly, if a backup application attempts to write a backup copy of your file over the disk-resident copy, and you explicitly deny write privileges to the backup application process, the restore operation cannot complete. In this case also, the backup application must be able to override the access control settings of your file.
L71: The SE_BACKUP_NAME and SE_RESTORE_NAME access privileges were specifically created to provide this ability to backup applications. If these privileges have been granted and enabled in the access token of the backup application process, it can then call 【8†CreateFile】 to open your file or directory for backup, specifying the standard READ_CONTROL access right as the value of the dwDesiredAccess parameter.
L72: However, to identify the calling process as a backup process, the call to CreateFile must include the FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS flag in the dwFlagsAndAttributes parameter. The full syntax of the function call is the following:
L73: 
L74:     `HANDLE hFile = CreateFile( fileName,                   // lpFileName
L75:                                READ_CONTROL,               // dwDesiredAccess
L76:                                0,                          // dwShareMode
L77:                                NULL,                       // lpSecurityAttributes
L78:                                OPEN_EXISTING,              // dwCreationDisposition
L79:                                FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS, // dwFlagsAndAttributes
L80:                                NULL );                     // hTemplateFile
L81:     `
L82: This will allow the backup application process to open your file and override the standard security checking. To restore your file, the backup application would use the following 【8†CreateFile】 call syntax when opening your file to be written.
L83: 
L84:     `HANDLE hFile = CreateFile( fileName,                   // lpFileName
L85:                                WRITE_OWNER | WRITE_DAC,    // dwDesiredAccess
L86:                                0,                          // dwShareMode
L87:                                NULL,                       // lpSecurityAttributes
L88:                                CREATE_ALWAYS,              // dwCreationDisposition
L89:                                FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS, // dwFlagsAndAttributes
L90:                                NULL );                     // hTemplateFile

L24: # Mandatory Integrity Control mechanism
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: ## In this article
L30: 
L31: Mandatory Integrity Control (MIC) provides a mechanism for controlling access to securable objects. This mechanism is in addition to discretionary access control and evaluates access before access checks against an object's 【5†discretionary access control list】 (DACL) are evaluated.
L32: MIC uses integrity levels and mandatory policy to evaluate access. 【6†Security principals】 and securable objects are assigned integrity levels that determine their levels of protection or access. For example, a principal with a low integrity level cannot write to an object with a medium integrity level, even if that object's DACL allows write access to the principal.
L33: Windows defines four integrity levels: low, medium, high, and system. Standard users receive medium, elevated users receive high. Processes you start and objects you create receive your integrity level (medium or high) or low if the executable file's level is low; system services receive system integrity. Objects that lack an integrity label are treated as medium by the operating system; this prevents low-integrity code from modifying unlabeled objects.
L34: Additionally, Windows ensures that processes running with a low integrity level cannot obtain access to a process which is associated with an app container.
L35: ## Integrity Labels
L36: 
L37: Integrity labels specify the integrity levels of securable objects and security principals. Integrity labels are represented by 【7†integrity SIDs】. The integrity SID for a securable object is stored in its 【6†system access control list】 (SACL). The SACL contains a 【8†SYSTEM_MANDATORY_LABEL_ACE】 【9†access control entry】 (ACE) that in turn contains the integrity SID. Any object without an integrity SID is treated as if it had medium integrity.
L38: The integrity SID for a security principal is stored in its access token. An access token may contain one or more integrity SIDs.
L39: 
L40: For detailed information about the defined integrity SIDs, see 【10†Well-known SIDs】.
L41: ## Process Creation
L42: When a user attempts to launch an executable file, the new process is created with the minimum of the user integrity level and the file integrity level. This means that the new process will never execute with higher integrity than the executable file. If the administrator user executes a low integrity program, the token for the new process functions with the low integrity level. This helps protect a user who launches untrustworthy code from malicious acts performed by that code.
L43: The user data, which is at the typical user integrity level, is write-protected against this new process.
L44: ## Mandatory Policy
L45: 
L46: The 【8†SYSTEM_MANDATORY_LABEL_ACE】 ACE in the SACL of a securable object contains an access mask that specifies the access that principals with integrity levels lower than the object are granted. The values defined for this access mask are SYSTEM_MANDATORY_LABEL_NO_WRITE_UP, SYSTEM_MANDATORY_LABEL_NO_READ_UP, and SYSTEM_MANDATORY_LABEL_NO_EXECUTE_UP. By default, the system creates every object with an access mask of SYSTEM_MANDATORY_LABEL_NO_WRITE_UP.
L47: Every access token also specifies a mandatory policy that is set by the 【11†Local Security Authority】 (LSA) when the token is created. This policy is specified by a 【12†TOKEN_MANDATORY_POLICY】 structure associated with the token. This structure can be queried by calling the 【13†GetTokenInformation】 function with the value of the TokenInformationClass parameter set to TokenMandatoryPolicy.
